questions.prompt: A composable draws with `Canvas(modifier) { drawRect(color) }`, where `color` is a `mutableStateOf(Color.Red)` read only inside the draw lambda. When `color` changes, which phases does Compose rerun for this node?

choices.text: Composition, layout and drawing, because every state change restarts the enclosing composable
Layout and drawing, because `Canvas` is a layout node
Only drawing, because the state was read during the drawing phase
None until the next configuration change, because draw lambdas are cached

sources.claim: State read during drawing (e.g. `drawRect(color)` inside `Canvas`) triggers only the drawing phase; reads in composition trigger recomposition, reads in measure/placement trigger layout and drawing.
sources.title: Jetpack Compose phases

questions.explanation: Compose tracks state reads per phase. A read inside a draw lambda is recorded in the drawing phase, so a change invalidates only drawing. The tempting answer (a) describes a read in the composable body, which would trigger recomposition; (b) describes a read in a measure/placement block such as `Modifier.offset { }`.

questions.prompt: A parallax header uses `Modifier.offset(with(LocalDensity.current) { (listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 2).toDp() })`. Layout Inspector shows the header recomposing on every scroll frame. Which change removes those recompositions while keeping the effect?

choices.text: Wrap the offset value in `remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }` and pass it to `Modifier.offset(dp)`
Mark the header composable `@Stable` so Compose skips it
Move the calculation into a `LaunchedEffect(listState)` that writes to another state
Use the lambda overload: `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 2) }`

sources.claim: Reading `listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset` inside `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(...) }` defers the read to the layout phase, so each scroll triggers only layout and drawing instead of recomposition.
sources.title: Jetpack Compose phases

sources.claim: When passing frequently changing State into modifiers, use the lambda versions of the modifiers whenever possible to defer reads.
sources.title: Follow best practices (Compose performance)

questions.explanation: The lambda overload of `offset` reads the scroll state during placement (layout phase), so a scroll only reruns layout and drawing. `derivedStateOf` does not help here: the derived value changes on every scroll pixel, so it is still read in composition and still recomposes. Writing to another state from an effect just moves the composition read elsewhere and adds a frame of lag.

questions.prompt: Code runs `Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { first.value = 1; second.value = 2 }` where both are `mutableStateOf` objects. When can other code observe the new values?

choices.text: After the block returns and the snapshot is applied; both changes then become visible atomically
Immediately after each assignment, one at a time, because `MutableState` writes are global
Only after `Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications()` is called explicitly from the block
Never outside the block: mutable snapshots are discarded when the block ends

sources.claim: All changes to state objects inside a mutable snapshot are isolated and not visible to other snapshots or as global state; `withMutableSnapshot` applies the snapshot when the block returns successfully, and after `apply` all changes are atomically visible.
sources.title: Snapshot.kt (Compose runtime source)

questions.explanation: A mutable snapshot isolates its writes: they are not visible to other snapshots or as global state until the snapshot is applied, and apply makes all of its changes visible atomically. `withMutableSnapshot` applies automatically when the block returns successfully. `sendApplyNotifications` is about writes made in the global snapshot, not a nested mutable snapshot.

questions.prompt: `Column { for (movie in movies) { MovieOverview(movie) } }` has no `key`. `MovieOverview` starts an image load in a `LaunchedEffect`. A new movie is inserted at the top of the list. What happens?

choices.text: Compose matches each instance to a movie by calling `movie.equals()` against the previous composition, so only the newly inserted item composes
Identified by call site plus order: every item shifts down, recomposes and restarts its effect
Nothing recomposes at all until the entire `Column` leaves and later re-enters the Composition, for example on a configuration change
Compose throws an exception at runtime, because duplicate call sites produced inside a loop always require explicit `key` blocks

sources.claim: When a composable is called multiple times from the same call site, Compose uses execution order to distinguish instances; inserting or reordering items makes affected instances recompose and restart side effects unless `key` provides identity.
sources.title: Lifecycle of composables

questions.explanation: Calls from the same call site in a loop are told apart only by execution order (positional memoization). Inserting at the top shifts every position, so each instance sees new inputs and its side effects restart. Wrapping the body in `key(movie.id) { ... }` gives each instance an identity that survives reordering. Compose does not match by `equals` without a key.

questions.prompt: An `Image` uses `Modifier.onSizeChanged { imageHeightPx = it.height }` and a following `Text` uses `Modifier.padding(top = imageHeightPx.toDp())`, where `imageHeightPx` is state. What does the user see?

choices.text: The text is placed with the correct padding in the very first frame, because the layout phase always finishes running before composition begins
An infinite recomposition loop that keeps rerunning forever and freezes the app on the very first frame
Frame 1 draws zero padding; the layout write schedules recomposition, so the text jumps a frame later
The write to `imageHeightPx` is silently ignored, because state writes of any kind are disallowed during the layout phase

sources.claim: Writing `imageHeightPx` from `onSizeChanged` and reading it for padding in composition causes frame 1 to use 0, recomposition to be scheduled from layout, and frame 2 to show correct padding: an extra frame and a visible jump; use proper layout primitives instead.
sources.title: Jetpack Compose phases

questions.explanation: This is a backward write across phases: layout writes state that composition already read. Frame 1 composes with the old value, the write during layout schedules recomposition, and frame 2 has the right padding, so the UI jumps. It does not loop forever because the size stabilises. The fix is a layout primitive or custom layout that measures both children together.

questions.prompt: A collapsing toolbar reads `scrollState.value` in its composable body to compute its height, alpha and offset, and the screen janks while scrolling. Explain Compose's three phases and how you would restructure this code so scrolling does not recompose the toolbar.

sources.claim: State reads in composition trigger recomposition, in layout trigger layout and drawing, and in drawing trigger only drawing; lambda modifiers like `Modifier.offset { }` defer reads to layout.
sources.title: Jetpack Compose phases

sources.claim: Pass a lambda such as `scrollProvider` and read it inside `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x = 0, y = scrollProvider()) }` to defer reads as long as possible.
sources.title: Follow best practices (Compose performance)

questions.explanation: A senior answer ties the fix to the mechanism (phase-scoped read tracking) rather than listing tricks, and knows that `derivedStateOf` does not fix a value that changes every frame. Mentioning the provider-lambda pattern shows experience with real toolbar code.

model_answer.summary: Compose runs composition (what), layout (measure and place) and drawing (how), and it tracks each state read against the phase where it happens. Reading scroll state in the body recomposes on every frame; defer the reads into layout and draw lambdas and pass providers instead of values.
key_points: Names the phases (composition, layout, drawing) and states that a state change reruns the phase where it was read, plus the later phases
Explains that a read in the composable body forces recomposition on every scroll frame, the most expensive option
Moves reads into lambda modifiers: `Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer { alpha = ... }`, `drawBehind { }` or a custom `layout { }`
Passes a provider lambda such as `scrollProvider: () -> Int` down the tree instead of the current value, so the read happens inside the child's layout/draw lambda
Verifies with Layout Inspector recomposition counts or a composition trace before and after

questions.prompt: Explain, at the level of the snapshot system, how a click handler setting `count.value++` on a `mutableStateOf` ends up recomposing only the composables that read `count`.

sources.claim: Snapshot read observers are called when a state object is read; apply notifications for state modified outside a snapshot are deferred until `sendApplyNotifications` is called; `registerApplyObserver` is called back when snapshots are applied to the global state.
sources.title: Snapshot.kt (Compose runtime source)

sources.claim: Any changes to `value` of a `MutableState` schedule recomposition of any composable functions that read `value`.
sources.title: State and Jetpack Compose

questions.explanation: The distinguishing detail is that Compose does not diff the UI: it knows exactly which scopes to rerun because it recorded reads. A strong answer connects read observers, apply notifications and invalidation, and notes that this is why non-observable mutable objects (a plain `ArrayList`) never trigger recomposition.

model_answer.summary: State objects live in the snapshot system. Compose records which state objects each scope reads through read observers, the write is published when the snapshot is applied (or when global apply notifications are sent), and apply observers let the runtime invalidate only the scopes that read the changed objects and schedule their recomposition.
key_points: While composing, the runtime observes reads (a read observer) and records which state objects each restartable scope read
A write to a state object is tracked by the snapshot system (write observer); changes in a mutable snapshot are isolated until applied, and applied changes become visible atomically
Writes made outside a mutable snapshot, such as in a click handler, have their apply notifications deferred until `Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications()` runs
Apply observers receive the set of changed objects; scopes that read them are invalidated and recomposed on the next frame, and other scopes are skipped

questions.prompt: In a `Column` built with `items.forEach { Row(item) }`, each row keeps an `expanded` flag in `remember`. After the user sorts the list, the expanded state appears on the wrong rows. Diagnose the cause and give the fix.

sources.claim: The call site identifies each composable instance; repeated calls from one call site use execution order; the `key` composable gives instances an explicit identity so they are recognised when order changes.
sources.title: Lifecycle of composables

questions.explanation: A senior candidate recognises the symptom as an identity problem, not a state bug, and also knows keys prevent unnecessary effect restarts, not only wrong state.

model_answer.summary: Compose identifies instances by call site and, inside a loop, by execution order. Remembered state is stored at a position, so sorting moves data but not state. Give each row an identity with `key(item.id)` (or use a Lazy list with `key =`).
key_points: Explains call-site identity: every call site is a distinct instance in the Composition
Explains positional memoization: repeated calls from one call site are distinguished only by execution order, so `remember` values stay at a position
Sorting changes which item is at each position, so the remembered `expanded` flag now belongs to a different item and effects restart
Fix: wrap each row in `key(item.id) { ... }` (or use `LazyColumn` with `key = { it.id }`) so state and effects move with the item

questions.prompt: The classes report shows `unstable class Snack { stable val id: Long; unstable val tags: Set<String> }`. Why is `Snack` unstable?

choices.text: Because `Set<String>` could be backed by a mutable implementation; Compose treats collection interfaces as unstable
Because `Long` is autoboxed to `java.lang.Long` on the JVM at runtime, and the compiler treats every boxed numeric type as unstable
Because every data class the compiler encounters is unstable by default until it is explicitly annotated with `@Immutable` or `@Stable`
Because `val` properties declared on a class can still be reassigned later at runtime through reflection, defeating the stability contract

sources.claim: The report shows `unstable val tags: Set<String>` making `Snack` unstable because the Compose compiler cannot be sure of immutability as it only sees the declared type.
sources.title: Diagnose stability issues

sources.claim: Compose always considers collection classes unstable, such as `List`, `Set` and `Map`; data classes with only `val` primitive properties are immutable.
sources.title: Stability in Compose

questions.explanation: The compiler only sees the declared type. `Set<String>` could be backed by a mutable set, so Compose always considers collection interfaces unstable, which makes the whole class unstable. A data class with only stable `val` properties (like `id: Long`) is inferred stable without any annotation. Fixes include kotlinx immutable collections (`ImmutableSet`) or a stability configuration.

questions.prompt: `data class User(val id: String, val name: String)` lives in a pure Kotlin `:core:model` module that does not apply the Compose compiler. In `:feature:profile`, the compiler report marks the `user: User` parameter as unstable. What is going on, and which fix is documented?

choices.text: Compose infers stability from linked bytecode at link time across all modules in the graph, so this particular report must simply be wrong; ignore it
The class must be rewritten as a regular class, since the compiler always treats data classes declared in other modules as inherently unstable
Only adding `@Immutable` inside `:feature:profile` through a local typealias around `User` can possibly fix this specific unstable-parameter warning
Modules the Compose compiler skips are unstable; apply it to `:core:model`, use a config file, or wrap in a UI model

sources.claim: Compose always considers classes unstable where they are from modules in which the Compose compiler does not run; wrap them in UI model classes if required.
sources.title: Stability in Compose

sources.claim: For multi-module apps: add classes to the stability configuration file, enable the Compose compiler on data-layer modules with only the Compose runtime dependency, or wrap data classes in UI-specific classes.
sources.title: Fix stability issues

questions.explanation: Stability inference only works for types in modules that the Compose compiler processed (or that are explicitly marked). The documented options are a stability configuration file, enabling the Compose compiler on the data module (runtime dependency only, no Compose UI), or wrapping the class in a UI-layer model. Annotations cannot be added from another module.

questions.prompt: With Strong Skipping enabled (the default since Kotlin 2.0.20), `ItemList(items: List<Item>)` has an unstable parameter. On each recomposition the parent passes `items = state.items.filter { it.visible }`, a new list with equal contents. Does `ItemList` skip?

choices.text: Yes, it skips: strong skipping compares every parameter, stable or not, with a structural `equals()` call regardless of its declared stability
No: unstable params use instance equality (`===`); `filter` returns a fresh instance each time
Yes, it skips: strong skipping mode simply ignores unstable parameters entirely when deciding whether a composable can be skipped
No, never: composables that declare even one unstable parameter remain permanently unskippable, even under strong skipping mode

sources.claim: With strong skipping, all restartable composables become skippable; unstable parameters are compared using instance equality (`===`) and stable parameters using `Object.equals()`; enabled by default in Kotlin 2.0.20.
sources.title: Strong skipping mode

questions.explanation: Strong skipping makes all restartable composables skippable, but it compares unstable parameters by instance identity and stable ones by `equals()`. A freshly filtered list is a new instance, so the check fails and `ItemList` recomposes. Fix it by computing the filtered list once (e.g. in the ViewModel or `remember(state.items)`) or by using an immutable collection type so `equals` is used.

questions.prompt: Under Strong Skipping, a composable passes `onClick = { viewModel.select(item) }` where `item` has an unstable type. What does the compiler generate for this lambda?

choices.text: Nothing at all: lambdas are only ever memoized automatically when every one of their captured values is already stable
A brand-new lambda instance is allocated on every single recomposition, so the child composable always recomposes
Wrapped in `remember(viewModel, item) { ... }`, with the unstable capture compared by instance equality
One static singleton lambda instance shared by every call site of this composable across the whole app

sources.claim: With strong skipping every lambda inside a composable is automatically remembered, wrapped in `remember` keyed by its captures; unstable keys are compared with instance equality and stable keys with object equality; `@DontMemoize` opts out.
sources.title: Strong skipping mode

questions.explanation: Strong skipping remembers every lambda inside a composable, keyed by its captures. Unstable keys are compared by instance equality and stable keys by object equality, so the lambda instance stays the same while `viewModel` and `item` are the same instances. Option (a) was the behaviour before strong skipping. `@DontMemoize` opts a lambda out.

questions.prompt: You add `composeCompiler { reportsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_compiler") }` to a module. Which output tells you whether the `SnackCollection` composable is restartable and skippable, and how should you build to get accurate results?

choices.text: `<module>-classes.txt`, from a debug build
The Layout Inspector recomposition column, from a debug build
`<module>-module.json` from `metricsDestination`, from any build type
`<module>-composables.txt` (or the `.csv` version), from a release build

sources.claim: `reportsDestination` produces `<module>-classes.txt` (class stability), `<module>-composables.txt` (restartable and skippable status) and `<module>-composables.csv`; always run on a release build for accurate results.
sources.title: Diagnose stability issues

questions.explanation: The composables report lists each composable with `restartable`/`skippable` markers and the stability of each parameter. The classes report explains class stability, which tells you why a parameter is unstable, but it does not tell you whether the function is skippable. The docs say to always run the reports on a release build.

questions.prompt: Explain what makes a type stable in Compose. Then compare three ways to make a UI model stable: making it truly immutable, annotating it with `@Immutable`/`@Stable`, and a stability configuration file. When is each appropriate and what are the risks?

sources.claim: A stable type must satisfy: `equals` results are forever the same for the same two instances, Composition is notified when a public property changes, and all public property types are stable.
sources.title: Lifecycle of composables

sources.claim: `@Stable`/`@Immutable` don't make a class stable on their own but opt into a contract, and incorrect annotation can break recomposition; prefer achieving stability without annotations; a stability configuration file can mark classes such as `java.time.LocalDateTime` stable.
sources.title: Fix stability issues

questions.explanation: A senior answer prefers structural fixes over annotations and can explain the failure mode of a wrong annotation. It also notes the docs warn against making everything skippable as a goal.

model_answer.summary: A stable type has consistent `equals`, notifies Composition when public properties change, and has only stable property types. Prefer real immutability; annotations and configuration files are promises the compiler trusts without checking, so a wrong promise produces stale UI.
key_points: States the three stability conditions: `equals` always returns the same result for the same two instances, Composition is notified when a public property changes, and all public property types are stable
Notes inferred cases: primitives, `String`, function types and `MutableState` are stable; `var` properties, interfaces and collection types like `List` make a class unstable
Real immutability: `val` properties, immutable types or kotlinx `ImmutableList`/`persistentListOf`, and Compose state (`mutableStateOf`) for anything that must change
`@Immutable`/`@Stable` are a contract, not enforcement; annotating a type that actually mutates can make recomposition skip and show stale data

Stability configuration file (`stabilityConfigurationFile`) for classes you do not own, such as `java.time.LocalDateTime` or a data module's package, with the same risk if the class is actually mutable

questions.prompt: After upgrading to Kotlin 2.0.20+, a colleague says: "Strong Skipping is on now, so stability doesn't matter any more." Evaluate that claim.

sources.claim: Strong skipping makes composables with unstable parameters skippable and remembers lambdas with unstable captures; unstable parameters use instance equality, stable ones use `equals`; opt out with `@NonSkippableComposable` or `@DontMemoize`; enabled by default in Kotlin 2.0.20.
sources.title: Strong skipping mode

questions.explanation: The strong candidate knows exactly what changed (skippability and lambda memoization) and what did not (the equality rule depends on stability), and gives a concrete case where identity comparison still fails.

model_answer.summary: Partly true: every restartable composable is now skippable and lambdas are remembered, but unstable parameters are compared by identity, so any unstable value recreated during recomposition still defeats skipping. Stability still decides whether `equals` or `===` is used.
key_points: Strong skipping is enabled by default since Kotlin 2.0.20 and makes all restartable composables skippable, even with unstable parameters

Unstable parameters are compared with `===` and stable ones with `equals()`; an unstable value rebuilt on each recomposition (a mapped or filtered list, a new wrapper object) still triggers recomposition
Lambdas are memoized with their captures as keys, so passing callbacks no longer needs manual `remember`, but an unstable capture that is a new instance each time still produces a new lambda
Opt-outs exist: `@NonSkippableComposable` for a function and `@DontMemoize` for a lambda
Stability still matters where equal-but-new values are common; fix with immutable types or by creating values once, and measure before optimising

questions.prompt: Walk through how you would find and fix unnecessary recompositions on one screen using Layout Inspector and Compose compiler reports. What would you avoid doing?

sources.claim: Layout Inspector shows recomposition and skip counts; compiler reports are enabled with `reportsDestination` and `metricsDestination`, should be run on release builds, and making your entire UI skippable is a premature optimisation.
sources.title: Diagnose stability issues

sources.claim: You shouldn't attempt to make every composable skippable; skip optimising composables that rarely recompose or only call other skippable composables.
sources.title: Fix stability issues

questions.explanation: The docs explicitly warn that making the whole UI skippable is premature optimisation. A senior answer is measurement-driven and names the specific report files and what each one tells you.

model_answer.summary: Find hot composables with Layout Inspector's recomposition and skip counts, generate compiler reports on a release build to see which parameters are unstable and why, apply the smallest fix, and re-measure. Avoid trying to make every composable skippable.
key_points: Use Layout Inspector recomposition and skip counts to find composables that recompose more than expected
Enable `reportsDestination`/`metricsDestination` in the `composeCompiler` block per module and build a release variant
Read `-composables.txt` for `restartable`/`skippable` and unstable parameters, and `-classes.txt` to see which property makes a class unstable
Apply a targeted fix: immutable collections, the Compose compiler on the data module, a stability configuration file, a UI wrapper model, or not recreating values during recomposition
Avoid premature optimisation: do not chase every unstable parameter or make everything skippable; fix only what measurements show matters

questions.prompt: A `FilterBar` and a `ResultsHeader` both display the selected filter, and only `FilterBar` changes it. Per the Compose state hoisting rules, where should the selected-filter state live?

choices.text: Inside `FilterBar` itself, which then exposes the current value to `ResultsHeader` by providing a `CompositionLocal`
At the lowest common parent, passed down as a value with an `onFilterChange` event going up
Duplicated separately inside both composables and kept in sync afterward with a `LaunchedEffect` observing each other
In a globally accessible singleton object, so that any composable anywhere in the tree can freely read and write it

sources.claim: State should be hoisted to at least the lowest common parent of all composables that read it and at least the highest level it may be changed; state goes down and events go up (unidirectional data flow).
sources.title: State and Jetpack Compose

questions.explanation: Hoist state to at least the lowest common parent of everything that reads it, and at least to the highest level where it is written. The parent passes the value down and receives events up (unidirectional data flow), giving a single source of truth. Duplicating state and syncing it with effects creates two sources of truth.

questions.prompt: A screen keeps `var filter by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(Filter(query = "", sort = Sort.Name)) }`, where `Filter` is a plain Kotlin data class. What must you do for this to work across activity recreation and process death?

choices.text: Nothing at all: `rememberSaveable` automatically serializes any Kotlin data class using reflection under the hood
Replace it with plain `remember(filter)` so the composition key itself survives activity recreation
Make it `Bundle`-storable, e.g. `@Parcelize`, or supply a `Saver` (`mapSaver`/`listSaver`)
Store the filter inside a `CompositionLocal` instead, since composition locals are documented to survive full process death

sources.claim: `rememberSaveable` retains state across activity or process recreation using the saved instance state mechanism; for types that can't be put in a Bundle use `@Parcelize`, `mapSaver` or `listSaver`.
sources.title: State and Jetpack Compose

questions.explanation: `rememberSaveable` persists through the saved instance state mechanism, so the value must be a type a `Bundle` can hold, or you provide a `Saver`. `remember` with keys only controls cache invalidation during composition; it does not survive recreation.

questions.prompt: `@Composable fun Splash(onTimeout: () -> Unit) { LaunchedEffect(onTimeout) { delay(3000); onTimeout() } }`. The parent recomposes often and passes a new lambda each time, so the timer keeps restarting. What is the documented fix?

choices.text: `val current by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)` and `LaunchedEffect(true) { delay(3000); current() }`
Replace `LaunchedEffect` with `SideEffect { }` so the timer runs after every recomposition
Use `DisposableEffect(onTimeout)` so the old timer is disposed correctly
Launch the timer from `rememberCoroutineScope()` directly in the composable body

sources.claim: `rememberUpdatedState` references a value in an effect that shouldn't restart if the value changes; the `LandingScreen` example uses `LaunchedEffect(true)` with `currentOnTimeout` so the timeout isn't restarted by recomposition.
sources.title: Side-effects in Compose

questions.explanation: The effect should follow the call site's lifecycle and not restart, but it must call the latest callback. `rememberUpdatedState` holds the newest `onTimeout` without being a key, and a constant key keeps the effect from restarting. `DisposableEffect(onTimeout)` has the same restart problem, and launching from a scope in the composable body runs on every recomposition.

questions.prompt: A composable must add a `LifecycleEventObserver` to `lifecycleOwner` and remove it when the composable leaves the Composition or `lifecycleOwner` changes. Which API fits?

choices.text: `SideEffect { lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer) }`
`LaunchedEffect(Unit) { lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer) }` and rely on coroutine cancellation to remove it
`remember { lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer) }`
`DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) { addObserver(observer); onDispose { removeObserver(observer) } }`

sources.claim: `DisposableEffect` is for side effects that need cleanup after keys change or the composable leaves the Composition, with a mandatory `onDispose`; the lifecycle observer example adds the observer and removes it in `onDispose`. `SideEffect` runs after every successful recomposition.
sources.title: Side-effects in Compose

questions.explanation: `DisposableEffect` is for effects that need cleanup when keys change or the composable leaves; `onDispose` is mandatory. `SideEffect` runs after every successful recomposition and has no cleanup, so it would add duplicate observers. Coroutine cancellation does not remove a lifecycle observer, and the `Unit` key would ignore a new `lifecycleOwner`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an appropriate use of `derivedStateOf`?

choices.text: `val fullName by remember { derivedStateOf { "$firstName $lastName" } }` for two text fields
`val showScrollToTop by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }`
`val total = derivedStateOf { price * quantity }` without `remember`, so it recomputes each time
`val user by remember { derivedStateOf { repository.loadUser() } }` to load data once

sources.claim: Use `derivedStateOf` when state changes more often than the UI needs to update, e.g. `listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0`; using it for `"$firstName $lastName"` is incorrect overhead.
sources.title: Side-effects in Compose

questions.explanation: `derivedStateOf` is useful when the input changes much more often than the result you care about: the index changes constantly while scrolling, but the boolean flips rarely, so readers recompose only on the flip. For `fullName` the output changes whenever an input changes, so the extra object is pure overhead. Loading data belongs in an effect or the ViewModel, not a derived state.

questions.prompt: Design the state for a search screen with a text field, a list of results and a ViewModel. Explain stateful vs stateless composables, unidirectional data flow, and where each piece of state should live.

sources.claim: Hoisting makes a composable stateless using a `value` and `onValueChange` pair; state should be hoisted to at least the lowest common parent of readers and highest writer, states changing on the same events together; hoisted state is single source of truth, shareable, interceptable and decoupled; state holders manage logic and state of composables.
sources.title: State and Jetpack Compose

questions.explanation: A senior answer uses the three hoisting rules precisely, distinguishes UI element state from screen state, and explains the testability win rather than stating UDF as a slogan.

model_answer.summary: Make the UI composables stateless (value in, events out), hoist UI state to the lowest common parent that reads it and the highest level that writes it, and keep screen/business state in the ViewModel or a state holder. State flows down, events flow up.
key_points: A stateless composable takes `value` and `onValueChange` (e.g. `SearchField(query, onQueryChange)`) and is easier to reuse, preview and test
Unidirectional data flow: state goes down as parameters, events go up as callbacks, giving one source of truth
Applies the hoisting rules: at least the lowest common parent of readers, at least the highest writer, and hoist states that change on the same events together
Business and screen state lives in the ViewModel; pure UI element logic can live in a plain state holder class created with `remember` (keyed where needed)
Benefits: the caller can intercept or modify events before changing state, and state can move to another layer without changing the composable
